b: Left HF: Results in pulmonary congestion , manifesting as dyspnea , orthopnea , paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) , and hemoptysis . The lung tissue often shows hemosiderin-laden macrophages (also known as heart failure cells ).

Right HF: The most common cause is left HF . Clinical signs include jugular venous distention (JVD) , peripheral edema , hepatomegaly , and ascites . The liver characteristically shows a nutmeg appearance .
Pressure overload (e.g., HTN, AS) leads to concentric hypertrophy , where sarcomeres are added in parallel.
Volume overload (e.g., AR, MR) leads to eccentric hypertrophy , where sarcomeres are added in series.

b: Symptoms: dyspnoea (exertional/orthopnoea/PND), fatigue, chest pain, palpitations, ankle swelling, weight gain, reduced exercise tolerance.
Exam findings: raised JVP, displaced apex, S3 gallop, bibasal crackles, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly, ascites, cool peripheries, tachycardia.
Cause-finding history: prior MI/IHD, hypertension, valvular disease, arrhythmias, alcohol use, thyroid disease, anaemia, infections (viral myocarditis), cardiotoxic drugs.

qs.q: A physician is delivering a complex treatment plan for heart failure to a patient with low health literacy. To ensure comprehension, the clinician should implement which of the following methods?
o: asking the patient to restate instructions in their words
providing a detailed medical journal for home reading
using advanced pharmacological terminology for precision
handing over a standard unillustrated consent form
relying entirely on pre-recorded audio instructions
qs.e: The teach-back method confirms patient understanding by having them explain the instructions back in their own words.

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with heart failure is started on spironolactone. Serum biochemistry shows rising potassium levels. What is the primary physiological site and mechanism of action of this diuretic agent?
o: Inhibition of the Na+-K+-2Cl- symporter in the thick limb
Antagonism of mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct
Blockade of epithelial sodium channels in the late tubule
Suppression of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Interference with sodium-chloride cotransporters in the tubule
qs.e: Spironolactone competitively antagonizes aldosterone at mineralocorticoid receptors in the cortical collecting duct.
qs.s: Weekly Pharmacology Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: An oncological regimen includes doxorubicin for a solid tumor. Years later, the patient develops signs of cardiomyopathy and heart failure. What is the fundamental mechanism of this cumulative cardiac toxicity?
o: Covalent DNA cross-linking in non-dividing myocardial cells
Depletion of intracellular carnitine stores for fatty acid oxidation
Inhibition of topoisomerase II alpha in adult cardiac myocytes
Direct intercalation into mitochondrial ribosomal RNA transcripts
Generation of reactive oxygen species via iron-mediated Fenton reactions
qs.e: Doxorubicin generates free radicals through iron-mediated mechanisms, causing cumulative lipid peroxidation and myocyte damage.
qs.s: Weekly Pharmacology Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A multiply transfused thalassemia patient develops sudden severe respiratory distress and hypoxemia during red cell infusion. Chest radiography reveals bilateral pulmonary infiltrates without heart failure. What is the diagnosis?
o: Severe anaphylactic shock with bronchospasm
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload
Transfusion-related acute lung injury
Acute respiratory distress from sepsis
Cardiogenic pulmonary edema from volume
qs.e: TRALI presents as non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema caused by donor antileukocyte antibodies activating recipient neutrophils.
qs.s: Weekly Year 3: Blood Transfusion Exam - November 20, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 50-year-old woman with breast cancer is given doxorubicin. Years later, she develops progressive heart failure. What is the primary molecular mechanism responsible for this anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity?
o: Generation of iron-mediated reactive oxygen species in cells with low catalase
Direct alkylation of mitochondrial DNA leading to permanent loss of myocytes
Inhibition of topoisomerase I causing widespread genomic double-strand breaks
Competitive blockade of beta-1 adrenergic receptors on the myocardial sarcolemma
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation via destruction of inner mitochondrial cristae
qs.e: Cardiomyocytes have low antioxidant enzyme levels and are exceptionally vulnerable to free radical generation and oxidative stress caused by doxorubicin.
qs.s: Weekly Pharmacology Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 67-year-old man with chronic heart failure presents with worsening peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, and an S3 gallop. His left ventricular ejection fraction is 30%. Which compensatory hemodynamic mechanism contributes most to his worsening fluid retention?
o: Enhanced vagal nerve stimulation suppressing heart rate
Upregulated atrial natriuretic peptide causing diuresis
Suppression of antidiuretic hormone release by pituitary
Decreased sympathetic tone reducing peripheral resistance
Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system
qs.e: Reduced cardiac output stimulates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, leading to systemic vasoconstriction and renal sodium retention.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Internal Medicine Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure presents with worsening dyspnea and orthopnea. BNP levels are markedly elevated. Which hemodynamic change primarily triggers BNP release?
o: Increased systemic vascular resistance and elevated afterload
Ventricular wall stretch resulting from volume overload
Reduced cardiac output and associated systemic hypotension
Sympathetic nervous system activation and resting tachycardia
Renal artery stenosis leading to decreased perfusion
qs.e: BNP is released from ventricular myocytes in response to increased wall stress and stretch caused by volume or pressure overload.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Internal Medicine Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 62-year-old man with chronic heart failure and fluid overload is prescribed a diuretic that inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Which agent matches this profile?
o: Bendroflumethiazide thiazide diuretic
Furosemide loop diuretic
Chlorthalidone thiazide‑like diuretic
Amiloride ENaC blocker
qs.e: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, providing potent natriuresis and diuresis. Bendroflumethiazide and chlorthalidone act on the distal convoluted tubule.
qs.s: Cardiovascular Pharmacology: Antihypertensive Drugs and Clinical: MCQs

es.q: A patient presents with acute liver injury secondary to severe right heart failure. Which acinar zone would you expect to be most affected and why?
es.m: Zone 3 (centrilobular) would be most affected. This zone has the worst oxygenation, making it highly susceptible to ischemic injury, as seen in conditions like right heart failure.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A 55-year-old male presents with signs of severe right heart failure. Which acinar zone is most likely to be affected by the resulting hepatic congestion and ischemia, and what is its characteristic oxygenation status?
es.m: Zone 3 (Centrilobular) is most likely to be affected. This zone is characterized by the worst oxygenation due to its location furthest from the portal triads and direct proximity to the central vein, making it highly susceptible to ischemic injury.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A patient presents with hepatic injury secondary to severe right heart failure. Which acinar zone would you expect to be primarily affected on histological examination, and what is the pathophysiological basis for this vulnerability?
es.m: Zone 3 (centrilobular) would be primarily affected. This zone is the furthest from the portal triads and thus receives the poorest oxygenation. In severe right heart failure, hepatic venous congestion leads to reduced blood flow and oxygen delivery, making Zone 3 particularly susceptible to hypoxic damage.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A patient with suspected liver dysfunction presents with severe right heart failure. Based on the liver's acinar organization, which specific zone is most vulnerable to injury in this scenario, and what are its characteristic features and oxygenation status?
es.m: In a patient with severe right heart failure, the most vulnerable zone is Zone 3, also known as the centrilobular zone. This zone is characterized by the worst oxygenation due to its farthest proximity from the portal triad's hepatic artery supply. It is specifically affected by conditions causing ischemia, shock, and right heart failure.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

rx.name: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

ai.clinicalScope: Chronic and acute heart failure in adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals, including common tropical co‑morbidities.
ai.title: Heart Failure
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Heart failure is a syndrome where the heart cannot pump enough blood, causing fluid buildup in the lungs and body. It is common in East Africa, often linked to hypertension, rheumatic disease, HIV, and limited diagnostic resources.

sections.p: Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome of impaired ventricular filling or ejection leading to insufficient tissue perfusion and/or congestion. In sub‑Saharan Africa prevalence is 1‑2 % in adults, rising to >10 % in those >65 yr, with higher rates in men and in patients with HIV or rheumatic heart disease.
b: Systolic HF: reduced ejection fraction (<40 %).
Diastolic HF: preserved ejection fraction (≥50 %) with abnormal filling.
Acute decompensated HF: rapid worsening of signs/symptoms requiring urgent treatment.
Right‑sided HF often follows left‑sided failure or primary pulmonary disease.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: Identify the precipitating pathology; in low‑resource settings infectious and rheumatic causes are prominent.
b: Hypertensive heart disease – leading cause of LV hypertrophy and systolic failure.
Rheumatic heart disease – mitral or aortic valve damage causing volume overload.
Ischaemic heart disease – prior MI or angina, increasingly common with urbanisation.
HIV‑associated cardiomyopathy – direct viral injury or antiretroviral toxicity.
Chronic anaemia (e.g., malaria, sickle cell) – high-output failure.
Peripartum cardiomyopathy – in women <6 months postpartum.

sections.p: Failure results from a mismatch between cardiac output and metabolic demand, triggering neuro‑hormonal activation that worsens congestion.
b: Reduced stroke volume → activation of sympathetic nervous system (↑ heart rate, vasoconstriction).
Renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system (RAAS) activation → sodium/water retention, ventricular remodeling.
Elevated natriuretic peptides (BNP/NT‑proBNP) reflect wall stress and attempt diuresis.
Ventilation‑perfusion mismatch from pulmonary congestion causes dyspnoea.
Systemic venous congestion leads to peripheral oedema, hepatic congestion, and renal dysfunction.

sections.p: Symptoms reflect congestion (pulmonary, systemic) and low output; presentation varies with left vs right dominance.
b: Dyspnoea on exertion, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea.
Fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance.
Bibasal crackles, wheeze (“cardiac asthma”).
Elevated jugular venous pressure, hepato‑jugular reflux.
Peripheral oedema, ascites, hepatomegaly.
Cold extremities, oliguria in low‑output states.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and exam quickly differentiate HF from primary pulmonary disease and uncover precipitants.
b: Ask about recent weight gain, nocturnal cough, orthopnoea, and medication adherence.
Enquire about hypertension, rheumatic fever, HIV status, recent infections, alcohol, and pregnancy.
Inspect for peripheral oedema, cachexia, and raised neck veins.
Palpate apex beat – displaced laterally in dilated LV, sustained in hypertrophy.
Auscultate: S3 gallop (volume overload), S4 (stiff ventricle), basilar crackles, murmurs of valvular disease.
Measure blood pressure in both arms; low systolic may indicate cardiogenic shock.

sections.p: Consider other causes of dyspnoea and oedema that mimic HF, especially where diagnostics are limited.
b: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) – wheeze, hyperinflation on CXR, smoking history.
Pulmonary tuberculosis – night sweats, weight loss, cavitary lesions.
Severe anaemia – high-output failure, pallor, low hemoglobin.
Nephrotic syndrome – massive oedema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia.
Pregnancy‑related oedema – symmetrical, resolves postpartum.
Pericardial tamponade – muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Prioritise tests that are available; interpret each in the clinical context.

t.b: Is there pulmonary congestion or cardiomegaly? → Cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions support HF; normal CXR suggests primary lung disease.
What electrical abnormalities are present? → LV hypertrophy, Q‑waves (old MI), atrial fibrillation (common precipitant).
Does the heart show reduced ejection fraction or pericardial effusion? → Visual estimate of EF, IVC size, B‑lines for pulmonary oedema; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs.
Is cardiac stretch elevated? → Values >100 pg/mL (BNP) or >300 pg/mL (NT‑proBNP) favour HF; low values make HF unlikely.

t.a: Full blood count, renal function, electrolytes
t.b: Are there anaemia, renal impairment, or electrolyte disturbances? → Guides diuretic safety and identifies co‑morbidities.
Is there acute myocardial injury? → Elevated troponin suggests acute coronary syndrome as trigger.

sections.p: Use the NYHA functional classification and the ACC/AHA stages to guide therapy and prognosis.
b: NYHA I – no limitation of physical activity.
NYHA II – slight limitation; comfortable at rest.
NYHA III – marked limitation; <ordinary activity causes symptoms.
NYHA IV – symptoms at rest.
ACC/AHA Stage A – at risk (e.g., hypertension).
Stage B – structural disease without symptoms.
Stage C – structural disease with current or prior symptoms.
Stage D – refractory HF requiring specialized interventions.

sections.p: Co‑existing conditions frequently alter presentation and management in low‑resource settings.
b: HIV infection – may cause myocarditis, interacts with some diuretics (nephrotoxicity).
Tuberculosis – pericardial involvement can mimic HF; consider pericardial effusion.
Malaria‑induced anaemia – high‑output failure; treat infection first.
Traditional herbal medicines – possible cardiotoxicity (e.g., aconite).
Limited laboratory capacity – rely on bedside assessment and simple tests.

sections.p: Treat precipitating cause, relieve congestion, and modify neuro‑hormonal activation; adapt to drug availability.
b: Stabilise airway, breathing, circulation; give supplemental O₂ if SpO₂ < 90 %.
Loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) IV bolus to reduce preload; monitor urine output.
If hypertension present, add ACE inhibitor or ARB (if available) to block RAAS.
Beta‑blocker (e.g., carvedilol) once euvolemic, to reduce sympathetic drive.
Spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist) for NYHA III–IV if potassium ≤5 mmol/L.
Treat underlying cause: anti‑TB therapy, antiretrovirals, antihypertensives, valve surgery referral.
Educate on low‑salt diet, fluid restriction (≤2 L/day), daily weight monitoring.
Arrange follow‑up within 1 week; arrange echocardiogram when feasible.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening decompensation and organ dysfunction.
b: Pulmonary oedema with severe hypoxia – requires urgent diuresis and possible non‑invasive ventilation.
Cardiogenic shock – hypotension, cool extremities, oliguria; consider inotropes if ICU available.
Renal failure – rising creatinine after diuretics; adjust dosing, consider renal‑sparing strategies.
Hyperkalaemia – from ACE‑I/ARB or spironolactone; stop offending drug, give calcium gluconate if ECG changes.
Thromboembolism – atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response; anticoagulation if INR monitoring possible.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and therapy for populations with unique physiology or co‑morbidities.
b: Pregnant women – avoid ACE‑I/ARB; use hydralazine + nitrates; monitor fetal growth.
Elderly – start diuretics low‑dose, watch for orthostatic hypotension.
HIV‑positive – watch for drug‑drug interactions with protease inhibitors; monitor CD4 and renal function.
Patients with sickle cell disease – high‑output failure; manage vaso‑occlusive crises and transfusion needs.

sections.p: Long‑term outcomes depend on stage, adherence, and control of risk factors.
b: 5‑year mortality 30‑50 % in stage C/D; better if hypertension controlled and no HIV.
Regular clinic visits every 1–3 months; repeat BNP or clinical scoring to gauge control.
Primary prevention: control blood pressure, treat rheumatic fever early, screen for HIV/TB.
Secondary prevention: lifestyle modification, medication adherence, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal).

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal in the local context.
b: BNP may be modestly elevated in severe anaemia; interpret with clinical picture.
Chest X‑ray can be normal early in acute decompensation; rely on bedside ultrasound if possible.
ECG may show LVH without HF; combine with symptoms before labeling.
Serum creatinine rises with diuretics; differentiate true renal injury from prerenal azotemia.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening breathlessness with chest pain or fainting
New onset rapid atrial fibrillation with heart rate >130 bpm

faq.q: Why is BNP useful in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: It rises quickly with ventricular stretch and helps differentiate cardiac from pulmonary causes when imaging is limited.
If caused by treatable conditions (e.g., hypertension, valve disease, infection) and caught early, ventricular function can improve markedly.

faq.q: What is the role of diuretics when kidneys are failing?
faq.a: Low‑dose loop diuretics may still relieve congestion; monitor urine output and avoid excessive volume depletion.

exam: A 58‑year‑old man with hypertension presents with orthopnoea and leg swelling. Which bedside sign most strongly supports left‑sided HF? — Presence of an S3 gallop indicating volume overload.

You have only a stethoscope and BP cuff. How would you differentiate cardiac asthma from COPD? — Look for elevated JVP, peripheral oedema, and a rapid response to diuretics; COPD shows prolonged expiratory wheeze without JVD.
A patient on furosemide develops a serum potassium of 5.8 mmol/L. What is your next step? — Stop potassium‑sparing agents, give calcium gluconate if ECG changes, and consider potassium‑binding resin.
Why are ACE inhibitors contraindicated in pregnancy but beneficial in HF? — They block RAAS, improving remodeling, but cause fetal renal dysgenesis; alternatives are hydralazine and nitrates.

In a HIV‑positive patient with HF, which medication interaction is most concerning? — Protease inhibitors can increase levels of certain diuretics and cause nephrotoxicity; monitor renal function closely.
A patient with NYHA class III HF has a BNP of 250 pg/mL. How does this influence management? — Confirms congestion; intensify diuretic regimen and consider adding aldosterone antagonist.
What is the first pharmacologic step in acute decompensated HF with pulmonary oedema? — IV loop diuretic bolus to reduce preload rapidly.

Explain why right‑sided HF often follows left‑sided failure. — Elevated left atrial pressure transmits backward to pulmonary circulation, increasing right ventricular afterload and causing systemic congestion.

A 30‑year‑old woman 4 months postpartum develops dyspnoea and an S3. What diagnosis should you consider and what is the initial therapy? — Peripartum cardiomyopathy; start diuretics, beta‑blocker once stable, and avoid ACE‑I until after delivery.

How would you manage HF in a setting without echocardiography? — Rely on clinical criteria (NYHA, Framingham), bedside ultrasound if available, BNP, and treat empirically while arranging referral for imaging.
What red‑flag symptom indicates possible progression to cardiogenic shock? — New onset confusion or altered mental status with hypotension and cold extremities.
